thread.title: There’s Still a Bull Case for FAANGs - Barron's

author: Teresa Rivas
title: There’s Still a Bull Case for FAANGs - Barron's
text:
By Teresa Rivas Aug. 3, 2018 10:31 a.m. ET While Apple (AAPL) was able to score a point for the FAANGs with its earnings, there's still some lingering investor worries about the group, given Facebook 's (FB) big fall and the protracted reign of tech's dominance.
Where we were : Tech has long led overall stocks higher, so concerns about the aging market is in large part a worry about how much longer tech can keep its winning streak going, which made Facebook's disappointment so jarring.
Where we're headed : Barron's has argued that the selloff is a buying opportunity, as does Fundstrat .
Illustration: Stefania M. D'Alessandro/Getty Images Now that Apple (AAPL) is worth a trillion dollars , it may be hard to remember all the way back to last week, when Facebook (FB) was plunging hard and dragging down the FAANG stocks –a group that expanded to include Apple from the original quartet of Facebook, Amazon.com (AMZN), Netflix (NFLX), and Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL)–with it.
Barron's argued that the steep selloff in Facebook is a buying opportunity , and Fundstrat 's Thomas Lee agrees . He writes that one of the biggest lessons we've leaned in the past decade is that markets have a tendency to overreact, and that if "such precedent plays out again, FANG stocks likely are presenting a buying opportunity here." Fundstrat, as indicated by its single-A "FANG," doesn't include Apple in its reckoning.
It's not hard to see the bull case for the group: Their growth rate is still three times the overall market, and their free cash flows are in line with the broader market, meaning that their valuations don't look "demanding."
Since 2004, the FANG stocks have contributed 10% to total top-line growth, Lee writes, even as the group's share of 2018 revenue growth is just 4%. "Think of the base effect here—FANG revs have compounded at 31% since 2004, compared to a 3.6% growth rate for the S&P 500 overall."
That growth stemmed from the growth of the internet, which has of course soared since 2004. But this phenomenon isn't new. Before it took hold as the major theme, the 1980s (and beyond) were dominated by consumer-spending growth, which rocketed higher and was the "Internet" narrative of that decade. The top seven large-cap consumer stocks, Walmart (WMT), Circuit City, Hasbro (HAS), Home Depot (HD), Gap (GPS), Limited Brands, and Dillard's (DDS) were the the FANGs of the 80s, appreciating 1,171 times from 1981 to 2000. Or, put another way, "FANG is a generational trade that followed on the heels of the exponential growth in internet."
Therefore, while today's tech giants still look attractive in Lee's book, he warns that they won't dominate the market forever. The next group of hot stocks, when it comes, will be dominated by millennials' needs, as they become the biggest and most influential generation.
Facebook is the only trading higher today, however, while the Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) is down 0.2% to $72.29 in morning trading.
